lesson.title: Where Derivatives Break Down
lesson.summary: A function fails to be differentiable at a point whenever the limit defining the derivative does not exist there, and this can happen in several distinct geometric ways.
lesson.body:
Differentiability is a stronger requirement than continuity, and there is more than one way for a function to fail it. By definition, f is differentiable at a if the limit of [f(a+h) - f(a)] / h as h approaches 0 exists as a single finite number. Whenever that limit fails to exist, whether because it does not settle down, because it blows up, or because the function is not even defined or continuous at the point, a is called a non-differentiable point of f. Recognizing the different ways this limit can fail is the key skill behind reading graphs, checking piecewise definitions, and avoiding the mistake of assuming every continuous function has a derivative everywhere.

The most basic reason a derivative can fail to exist is that the function itself is not continuous at the point. If f has a jump discontinuity, a removable hole, or an infinite discontinuity at a, then the difference quotient cannot converge to a finite limit, because f(a+h) does not even approach f(a) as h shrinks. This case is easy to rule out first: continuity is a necessary condition for differentiability, so checking continuity at a suspicious point is always the first step before worrying about slopes.

Even when a function is continuous, the one-sided derivatives from the left and right can simply disagree, both existing as finite numbers but pointing in different directions. This produces a sharp bend in the graph called a corner point, and it is the situation examined in detail using one-sided derivatives, such as f(x) = |x| at x = 0, where the left-hand derivative is -1 and the right-hand derivative is 1.

A second way continuity survives while differentiability fails is when the one-sided derivatives are not finite at all. If the difference quotient grows without bound as h shrinks from both sides, the tangent line becomes vertical, and depending on whether the two sides diverge to the same infinite sign or to opposite infinite signs, the graph shows either a vertical tangent point or a sharp cusp. As a preview, the function f(x) = x^(1/3) has a vertical tangent at x = 0 because its slope diverges to positive infinity from both sides, while f(x) = the square root of the absolute value of x has a cusp there because the slope diverges to negative infinity from the left and positive infinity from the right.

To test whether a specific point is a point of non-differentiability, a reliable checklist works well: first confirm the function is continuous there, since discontinuity settles the question immediately. If it is continuous, compute the left-hand and right-hand derivatives separately. If they exist and agree, the function is differentiable with that common value as the derivative. If they exist but disagree, the graph has a corner. If either one-sided derivative diverges to infinity, examine whether the two sides share the same sign, which distinguishes a vertical tangent from a cusp. This same checklist reappears, applied in detail, for each of the specific cases in the sections that follow.
